title: Simplex Diffusion Models

paper.title: Simplex Diffusion Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion models have revolutionized generative modeling for continuous data through the gradual refinement of a belief state. This iterative refinement has not yet carried over to discrete diffusion models, which discard uncertainty at intermediate steps through categorical sampling ( information collapse ).
We propose Simplex Diffusion Models (SDMs), a framework that lifts the diffusion process to the probability simplex to represent beliefs over categories. SDMs admit probability paths with closed-form reverse transitions and can be trained with a simple cross-entropy loss. Contrary to earlier proposals such as Dirichlet Flow Matching which requires integrating an ordinary differential equation, we introduce a DDIM-like sampler with a tunable level of stochasticity. Because SDMs operate on samples on the simplex, they can carry uncertainty across denoising steps, which mitigates information collapse.
On OpenWebText, SDMs are competitive with strong Discrete Diffusion baselines, achieving 17.0 17.0 GenPPL at 5.46 5.46 unigram entropy in 64 sampling steps, close to real validation data.
Even without Self-Conditioning (SC), SDMs outperform masked and uniform diffusion (with SC or predictor-corrector sampling) on code generation (TinyGSM, T = 0.1 T=0.1 ; 49.0 % 49.0\% vs. 45.8 % 45.8\% ).
Distilled down to 8 steps, SDMs solve 32.1 % 32.1\% of GSM8K problems, more than distilled Discrete Diffusion models with 128 steps ( 21.4 % 21.4\% ).

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Denoising diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021b ) are state-of-the-art generative models in continuous domains ( Ho et al., 2022 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Ramesh et al., 2022 ; Watson et al., 2023 ) . However, a vast portion of real-world data—including text, biological sequences, and graph structures—is discrete, and extending diffusion to those modalities remains challenging ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Hoogeboom et al., 2021 ; Campbell et al., 2022 ) . Existing diffusion models for categorical data generally fall into three categories. First, categorical diffusion models such as masked or uniform diffusion models ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ; Ou et al., 2025 ) define the corruption process directly on sequences of discrete tokens. While theoretically sound, they suffer from information collapse . Indeed, as intermediate states are discrete, the denoiser’s uncertainty is discarded at each update. Hence, these models rely on Self-Conditioning ( Chen et al., 2022 ) or loopholing ( Jo et al., 2026 ) to carry beliefs across sampling steps. Second, continuous relaxations diffuse one-hot vectors ( Lee et al., 2026 ; Roos et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026 ) , learned embeddings ( Dieleman et al., 2022 ; Gulrajani & Hashimoto, 2023 ; Deschenaux & Gulcehre, 2026 ; Chemseddine et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) , or frozen embeddings ( Hu et al., 2026 ; Shen et al., 2026 ) . However, the identity of the clean category tends to be destroyed abruptly, within a short window during the forward process, and this worsens as the dimension of the encoding grows ( Pynadath et al., 2026a ; Shabalin et al., 2026 ) . Finally, a third line of work diffuses directly on the probability simplex, whose elements are distributions over categories ( Richemond et al., 2022 ; Cheng et al., 2024 ; Davis et al., 2024 ; Stark et al., 2024 ; Cheng et al., 2025 ; Williams et al., 2026 ; Boget & Kalousis, 2026 ; Chandra et al., 2026 ) . However, they typically sample by numerically integrating an ODE or SDE: Dirichlet Flow Matching (DFM; Stark et al., 2024 ), the closest to our work, scales poorly to large vocabularies ( Table 3 ). While the concurrent Simplax model ( Sakurai et al., 2026 ) does not rely on numerical integration, their sampling procedure operates on categorical samples rather than the continuous representation itself.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: We propose Simplex Diffusion Models (SDMs), whose intermediate states are distributions over tokens. 1. Similar to DFM, SDMs use a Dirichlet forward process, but parameterized so that its mean and concentration are set separately. This path admits closed-form reverse transitions, inducing a DDIM-style sampler ( Song et al., 2021a ) , with a churn parameter that controls the sampling stochasticity. SDMs are trained with a simple cross-entropy objective. Because SDMs operate on samples on the simplex, they can carry uncertainty across denoising steps, mitigating information collapse. 2. We show that SDMs unify discrete and continuous diffusions. A category sampled from the diffused simplex state has the same marginal distribution as if it were corrupted by Discrete Diffusion ( Section 3.1 ). Viewing the inverse Dirichlet concentration as a temperature , SDMs reduce to Discrete Diffusion at high temperature, and follow a deterministic path with Gaussian fluctuations at low temperature ( Section 4.1 and Section E.7 ). 3. Empirically, even without Self-Conditioning (SC), SDMs outperform masked and uniform diffusion (using either SC or predictor-corrector sampling) on TinyGSM ( T = 0.1 T=0.1 ; 49.0 % 49.0\% vs. 45.8 % 45.8\% ; Figure 1 ). Distilled down to 8 steps, SDMs solve 32.1 % 32.1\% of the GSM8K problems, more than distilled Discrete Diffusion models with 128 steps ( 21.4 % 21.4\% ; Table 5 ). On Sudoku, SDMs with SC match the best Discrete Diffusion model ( 99.1 % 99.1\% vs. 99.3 % 99.3\% ). On OpenWebText, SDMs are competitive with UDM and MDMs with all those methods achieving a GenPPL/Entropy frontier that matches real data after logit shaping interventions. This result calls into question the validity of OpenWebText in assessing the unconditional text generation capabilities of small scale models. We also validate the flexibility of our approach by achieving competitive performance on quality and diversity metrics for molecule generation, see Section K.7 .

sections.heading: Experimental Setup.
sections.text: We train on 200k grids with 30/81 clues revealed and evaluate on 5k unseen examples. We train a modified Diffusion Transformer (DiT) ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) as in Lou et al. (2024) with embedding dimension 512, 8 layers and 8 attention heads (28.6M parameters) for 50k steps. We use 180 sampling steps for the diffusion variants. See Section J.4 for further details.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: SDMs are the strongest continuous method on Sudoku and match the Discrete Diffusion models ( Table 1 ). Without Self-Conditioning (SC), SDMs outperform MDMs and UDMs with ancestral sampling and FLMs, and match 𝕊 \mathbb{S} -FLMs. With SC, SDMs reach 99.1%, outperforming the continuous baselines and within 0.2 points of the best result overall. SDMs also outperform Dirichlet Flow Matching (DFM) by a wide margin (76.7%; Table 2 ). Setting κ = 1 \kappa=1 works best. Without SC, increasing κ \kappa from 0 0 to 1 1 improves the accuracy from 73.9% to 88.4% ( Tables 21 , 22 and 23 ). With SC, SDMs perform similarly across churns. Training with the adaptive time sampler ( Section J.1 ) generally improves MDMs, UDMs, and SDMs at low churn.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup.
sections.text: We train on TinyGSM, a dataset of 11.8M synthetic math word problems with executable Python solutions, and evaluate on the GSM8K test set by executing one generated solution per problem. We tokenize with the SmolLM tokenizer, and use a context length of 512. We train a 12-layer DiT with hidden dimension 768 and 12 attention heads (167.9M parameters) for 250k steps ( ≈ 77 % \approx 77\% for SC variants, to match the training FLOPs; Section I.3 ) with a batch size of 512. See Section J.5 for further details. With ODE sampling, FLM, 𝕊 \mathbb{S} -FLM and DFM perform worse than the discrete baselines on TinyGSM, so we defer them to Appendix K .

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: We compare SDMs against MDMs and UDMs with the ancestral sampler, with a Predictor-Corrector (PC) sampler ( Section I.2 ) and with Self-Conditioning (SC; Section I.3 ). Since the expected embedding is costly with a large vocabulary, we also train SDMs that embed only the token argmax ​ P t \mathrm{argmax}~P_{t} , optionally combined with SC (Argmax + SC; Section J.2 ). With the expected embedding and without SC, SDMs outperform all diffusion baselines at 512 steps ( Figure 1 ), reaching 45.8 % 45.8\% at T = 1 T=1 (vs. 36.8 % 36.8\% for UDM + PC) and 49.0 % 49.0\% at T = 0.1 T=0.1 (vs. 45.8 % 45.8\% for MDM + SC). With Argmax + SC, SDMs perform best at T = 0.1 T=0.1 from 32 function evaluations (NFE) onward and reach 57.0 % 57.0\% at 8k NFE ( 50.2 % 50.2\% at 512 NFE). Chemseddine et al. (2026) train Spherical Flow (SF) with the same setup and find that PC sampling and SC are essential. With 512 NFE ( T = 1 T=1 ), the accuracy increases from 6.4 % 6.4\% with ODE sampling to 41.7 % 41.7\% with PC and SC. In this setting, SDMs without SC outperform SFs without SC ( 45.8 % 45.8\% vs. 32.4 % 32.4\% ) and perform similarly to SFs with SC ( Table 4 ).

sections.heading: Experimental Setup.
sections.text: We train on OWT ( Gokaslan & Cohen, 2019 ) for unconditional language modeling, and evaluate the generation quality via Generative Perplexity (GenPPL) under a pretrained GPT-2-large model ( Radford et al., 2019 ) alongside unigram entropy ( H 1 H_{1} ). We tokenize with the GPT-2 tokenizer, and use a context length of 1024. We train a 12-layer DiT with hidden dimension 768 and 12 attention heads (167.9M parameters) for 1M steps with a batch size of 512.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: With a few sampling interventions that improve the diffusion variants (MDMs, UDMs and SDMs), SDMs reach the same Pareto frontier as MDMs and UDMs. Similar interventions also improve AR models, whose frontier reaches the real OWT validation data. These results highlight that heuristic optimization can surpass the empirical validation point of OWT through simple logit shaping, thereby illustrating the limitation of generative frontiers ( Pynadath et al., 2026b ) . We briefly describe the four logit shaping interventions we introduce. First, we consider top-p sampling as in Holtzman et al. (2019) . Second we introduce a power-law logit temperature annealing during sampling similarly to DiffusionGemma Team et al. (2026) ; Chang et al. (2022) . The third intervention which is by far the most impactful is a sequence frequency penalty , see ( 184 ) and ( 185 ) for more details. Note that this intervention benefits all experimental setups including MDM, UDM, SDM and AR. Finally, SDM is the only model to benefit from a local frequency penalty which bridges the gap between SDMs and state-of-the-art MDM and UDM for text generation, achieving a GenPPL/Entropy trade-off that is close to real validation data (GenPPL/Entropy: 17.0 17.0 / 5.46 5.46 ). More details on the interventions and additional results can be found in Section K.5 . Our main results including the Pareto frontiers for all models we consider are presented in Figure 3 . Non-cherry picked samples are shown in Appendix L . Finally, in Section K.6 , we present additional non-generative evaluation results on language understanding by evaluating our models on ARC-easy ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) and HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) . sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper introduces Simplex Diffusion Models (SDMs) for discrete data. Unlike standard Discrete Diffusion models, SDMs can maintain a continuous distributional belief state throughout the generative process, circumventing information collapse even without Self-Conditioning, with which SDMs remain complementary. Our proposed generative model introduces a flexible DDIM-type sampler that does not require discretizing an ODE or SDE. When compared to strong baselines, SDMs are competitive on unconditional text generation and molecular synthesis, and state-of-the-art on coding. Nevertheless, our experiments remain limited to small models, and whether these conclusions remain valid at scale is an open question. Further experimentation is needed to assess the viability of the approach on large-scale language generation tasks. More broadly, SDMs suggest that there is a false dichotomy between discrete and continuous diffusion language models. Discrete Diffusion Models emerge at the high temperature limit, and with the Argmax input ( Section J.2 ), the denoiser processes a discrete sequence, while the generative process itself remains continuous on the simplex.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: To ensure the full reproducibility of our theoretical and empirical results, we provide comprehensive documentation across the paper and its supplementary material: • Theoretical Claims and Proofs: Complete mathematical proofs for all propositions ( Sections 3.1 , 3.1 , 3.1 and 4.1 ) and extended results, including Gaussian fluctuation limits ( Section E.7 ), the variational lower bound ( Appendix F ), and Simplex DMD distillation ( Appendix G ), are provided in Appendix E , Appendix F , Appendix G , with all mathematical assumptions explicitly stated. • Algorithms and Pseudocode: Self-contained algorithmic pseudocode is detailed in Algorithm 1 (Training), Algorithm 2 (Inference), Algorithm 3 (Accelerated Marsaglia–Tsang Gamma Sampling; see also Appendix D ), and Algorithm 4 (Simplex Distribution Matching Distillation), along with multi-token and classifier-free guidance extensions in Sections C.1 and C.2 . • Model Architectures and Hyperparameters: Detailed neural network architectures (Diffusion Transformer configurations, layer counts, embedding dimensions, attention heads), optimizer parameters (Adam/AdamW learning rates, warmup, EMA decay, gradient clipping), adaptive time schedules ( Section J.1 ), denoiser input parameterizations ( Section J.2 ), and variance schedules ( ν t \nu_{t} ; Section 4.2 ) are specified in Sections J.1 , J.2 , J.4 , J.5 , J.7 and J.8 . • Experimental Details and Full Sweeps: Full experimental ablations and hyperparameter sweeps are documented in Appendix K and in the full result tables ( Tables 21 , 22 , 23 , 29 , 31 , 30 and 32 ), including exact mean and standard deviation values across random seeds.

sections.heading: A.1 Basic Definitions
sections.text: For sake of completeness, we recall elementary facts about the Beta, Dirichlet and Gamma distributions. The Beta distribution is a distribution on [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Given a , b > 0 a,b>0 , the associated Beta density Beta ⁡ ( x , a , b ) \mathrm{Beta}(x;a,b) is given for any x ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] x\in[0,1] by Beta ⁡ ( x , a , b ) = Γ ⁡ ( a + b ) Γ ⁡ ( a ) ​ Γ ​ ( b ) ​ x a − 1 ​ ( 1 − x ) b − 1 , \mathrm{Beta}(x;a,b)=\frac{\Gamma(a+b)}{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1}, (22) where Γ ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \Gamma(\cdot) is the Gamma function. The Dirichlet distribution is a distribution on the simplex Δ N \Delta_{N} . Given β = ( β 1 , … , β N ) \beta=(\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{N}) , the associated Dirichlet density Dir ⁡ ( P , β ) \mathrm{Dir}(P;\beta) is given for any P ∈ Δ N P\in\Delta_{N} by Dir ⁡ ( P , β ) = Γ ⁡ ( ∑ i = 1 N β i ) ∏ i = 1 N Γ ⁡ ( β i ) ​ ∏ i = 1 N p i β i − 1 , \mathrm{Dir}(P;\beta)=\frac{\Gamma(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\beta_{i})}{\prod_{i=1}^{N}\Gamma(\beta_{i})}\prod_{i=1}^{N}p_{i}^{\beta_{i}-1}, (23) We have 𝔼 ⁡ [ P ] = P ¯ = ( β 1 C , … , β N C ) , Cov ⁡ [ P ] = diag ​ ( P ¯ ) − P ¯ ​ P ¯ ⊤ C + 1 , \mathbb{E}[P]=\bar{P}=\left(\frac{\beta_{1}}{C},\dots,\frac{\beta_{N}}{C}\right),\quad\operatorname{Cov}[P]=\frac{\text{diag}(\bar{P})-\bar{P}\bar{P}^{\top}}{C+1}, (24) where C = ∑ i = 1 N β i C=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\beta_{i} the concentration parameter of the Dirichlet distribution. The Gamma distribution is a distribution on [ 0 , ∞ ) [0,\infty) defined for parameters α , β > 0 \alpha,\beta>0 by Gamma ⁡ ( x , α , β ) = β α Γ ⁡ ( α ) ​ x α − 1 ​ exp ⁡ ( − β ​ x ) . \mathrm{Gamma}(x;\alpha,\beta)=\frac{\beta^{\alpha}}{\Gamma(\alpha)}x^{\alpha-1}\exp(-\beta x). (25) We will use extensively in practice the following fact. For N N independently distributed Gamma random variables X 1 ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( α 1 , 1 ) , ⋯ , X N ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( α N , 1 ) X_{1}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_{1},1),\cdots,X_{N}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_{N},1) , we have P = ( X 1 ∑ i = 1 N X i , ⋯ , X N ∑ i = 1 N X i ) ∼ Dir ⁡ ( α 1 , ⋯ , α N ) . P=\left(\frac{X_{1}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}},\cdots,\frac{X_{N}}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}X_{i}}\right)\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha_{1},\cdots,\alpha_{N}). (26) We will use the following convention throughout. Whenever a Gamma/Beta/Dirichlet parameter lies on the boundary (for instance, some Dirichlet coordinates are zero, or a formula is obtained as the limit t ↓ 0 t\downarrow 0 ), the corresponding distribution is understood in the natural degenerate/weak-limit sense. In particular, Dirichlet distributions with some zero coordinates are supported on the corresponding face of the simplex, Beta distributions with a zero parameter are degenerate at 0 0 or 1 1 , and formulas involving t = 0 t=0 are interpreted as limits of the same formulas for t > 0 t>0 .

sections.heading: A.2 Some Useful Properties of Dirichlet Distributions
sections.text: We now recall two simple results for Dirichlet distributions. To keep the paper self-contained, we provide proofs below without any claim of originality. Proposition A.1 (Sum of Dirichlet random variables): Let α , β ∈ ℝ N \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}^{N} with β i ≥ α i ≥ 0 \beta_{i}\geq\alpha_{i}\geq 0 for any i ∈ { 1 , … , N } i\in\{1,\dots,N\} and assume that X ∼ Dir ⁡ ( α ) X\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha) . Denote γ = β − α \gamma=\beta-\alpha and let W ∼ Beta ⁡ ( ∑ i = 1 N α i , ∑ i = 1 N γ i ) W\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_{i},\sum_{i=1}^{N}\gamma_{i}) independent of X X . Let V ∼ Dir ⁡ ( γ ) V\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\gamma) , independent of X X and W W . Finally, let Y Y be given by Y = W ​ X + ( 1 − W ) ​ V . Y=WX+(1-W)V. (27) Then, we have that Y ∼ Dir ⁡ ( β ) Y\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\beta) . Proof. Using the Gamma \mathrm{Gamma} characterization of Dirichlet random variables, there exist independent random variables ( Z i ) i = 1 N (Z_{i})_{i=1}^{N} such that Z i ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( α i , 1 ) Z_{i}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_{i},1) and X = ( Z i / ∑ j = 1 N Z j ) i = 1 N X=\left(Z_{i}/\sum_{j=1}^{N}Z_{j}\right)_{i=1}^{N} . Similarly, there exist independent random variables ( Z i ′ ) i = 1 N (Z_{i}^{\prime})_{i=1}^{N} such that Z i ′ ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( γ i , 1 ) Z_{i}^{\prime}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\gamma_{i},1) and V = ( Z i ′ / ∑ j = 1 N Z j ′ ) i = 1 N V=\left(Z_{i}^{\prime}/\sum_{j=1}^{N}Z_{j}^{\prime}\right)_{i=1}^{N} . We denote Z ¯ = ∑ i = 1 N Z i \bar{Z}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i} , Z ¯ ′ = ∑ i = 1 N Z i ′ \bar{Z}^{\prime}=\sum_{i=1}^{N}Z_{i}^{\prime} , and W = Z ¯ / ( Z ¯ + Z ¯ ′ ) W=\bar{Z}/(\bar{Z}+\bar{Z}^{\prime}) . Note that Z ¯ \bar{Z} and Z ¯ ′ \bar{Z}^{\prime} are independent of each other and independent of V V and X X . The random variable W W is independent of X X and V V by Lukacs’s Proportion-Sum Independence Theorem, see Ng et al. (2011) . In addition, Z ¯ ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( ∑ i = 1 N α i , 1 ) \bar{Z}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_{i},1) and Z ¯ ′ ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( ∑ i = 1 N γ i , 1 ) \bar{Z}^{\prime}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\gamma_{i},1) using the summation property of independent Γ \Gamma distributions. Now using the characterization of Beta \mathrm{Beta} distributions with Gamma \mathrm{Gamma} distributions, we get that W ∼ Beta ⁡ ( ∑ i = 1 N α i , ∑ i = 1 N γ i ) W\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\sum_{i=1}^{N}\alpha_{i},\sum_{i=1}^{N}\gamma_{i}) . Finally, we have that Y = W ​ X + ( 1 − W ) ​ V = ( Z i + Z i ′ ∑ j = 1 N ( Z j + Z j ′ ) ) i = 1 N . Y=WX+(1-W)V=\left(\frac{Z_{i}+Z_{i}^{\prime}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}(Z_{j}+Z_{j}^{\prime})}\right)_{i=1}^{N}. (28) We conclude the proof using the summation property of independent Γ \Gamma random variables and the Γ \Gamma characterization of Dirichlet random variables. ∎ Proposition A.2 (Dirichlet thinning): Let X ∼ Dir ⁡ ( α ) X\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha) with α ∈ ℝ N \alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{N} with α i ≥ 0 \alpha_{i}\geq 0 for any i ∈ { 1 , … , N } i\in\{1,\dots,N\} . The construction has to be understood on the supporting face I = { i : α i > 0 } I=\{i:\alpha_{i}>0\} ; coordinates outside I I are fixed at zero and omitted from the normalization. For ρ ∈ ( 0 , 1 ] \rho\in(0,1] and i ∈ I i\in I , let B i ∼ Beta ⁡ ( ρ ​ α i , ( 1 − ρ ) ​ α i ) B_{i}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\rho\alpha_{i},(1-\rho)\alpha_{i}) be mutually independent random variables, also independent of X X , and define Y Y by Y i = B i ​ X i ∑ j ∈ I B j ​ X j for ​ i ∈ I , Y i = 0 for ​ i ∉ I . Y_{i}=\frac{B_{i}X_{i}}{\sum_{j\in I}B_{j}X_{j}}\quad\text{for }i\in I,\qquad Y_{i}=0\quad\text{for }i\notin I. (29) Then Y ∼ Dir ⁡ ( ρ ​ α ) Y\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\rho\alpha) . Proof. By restricting to the supporting face and relabelling its coordinates, it is enough to consider α i > 0 \alpha_{i}>0 for every i ∈ { 1 , … , N } i\in\{1,\dots,N\} . We sample mutually independent variables Z i ∼ Γ ⁡ ( α i , 1 ) Z_{i}\sim\Gamma(\alpha_{i},1) and B i ∼ Beta ⁡ ( ρ ​ α i , ( 1 − ρ ) ​ α i ) B_{i}\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\rho\alpha_{i},(1-\rho)\alpha_{i}) , and define X = ( Z i / ∑ j = 1 N Z j ) i = 1 N X=(Z_{i}/\sum_{j=1}^{N}Z_{j})_{i=1}^{N} . This defines the joint distribution of ( X , ( B i ) i = 1 N ) (X,(B_{i})_{i=1}^{N}) . For any i ∈ { 1 , … , N } i\in\{1,\dots,N\} , let Z i ′ = Z i ​ B i Z_{i}^{\prime}=Z_{i}B_{i} and we have that Y = ( B i ​ X i ∑ j = 1 N B j ​ X j ) i = 1 N = ( B i ​ Z i ∑ j = 1 N B j ​ Z j ) i = 1 N = ( Z i ′ ∑ j = 1 N Z j ′ ) i = 1 N . Y=\left(\frac{B_{i}X_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}B_{j}X_{j}}\right)_{i=1}^{N}=\left(\frac{B_{i}Z_{i}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}B_{j}Z_{j}}\right)_{i=1}^{N}=\left(\frac{Z_{i}^{\prime}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}Z_{j}^{\prime}}\right)_{i=1}^{N}. (30) We now use the fact that for independent random variables A ∼ Beta ⁡ ( b , a − b ) A\sim\mathrm{Beta}(b,a-b) and B ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( a , 1 ) B\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(a,1) then A ​ B ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( b , 1 ) AB\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(b,1) , using Lukacs’s Proportion-Sum Independence Theorem, see Ng et al. (2011) . So for any i ∈ { 1 , … , N } i\in\{1,\dots,N\} , with A = B i A=B_{i} , B = Z i B=Z_{i} , a = α i a=\alpha_{i} and b = ρ ​ α i b=\rho\alpha_{i} . It follows that that ( Z i ′ ) i = 1 N (Z_{i}^{\prime})_{i=1}^{N} is a collection of independent random variables such that Z i ′ ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( ρ ​ α i , 1 ) Z_{i}^{\prime}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\rho\alpha_{i},1) . Therefore, using once again the Gamma \mathrm{Gamma} representation of Dirichlet random variables, Y ∼ Dir ⁡ ( ρ ​ α ) Y\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\rho\alpha) . ∎

sections.heading: C.1 Extension to Multiple Tokens
sections.text: So far, we have presented Simplex Diffusion Models for a single token taking values in 𝒳 = { 1 , … , N } \mathcal{X}=\{1,\dots,N\} . We now discuss how to extend the construction to sequences x 0 = ( x 0 1 , … , x 0 L ) ∈ 𝒳 L x_{0}=(x_{0}^{1},\dots,x_{0}^{L})\in\mathcal{X}^{L} . To obtain a scalable solution, we consider a product of simplices and represent the state at time t t by P t = ( P t 1 , … , P t L ) ∈ ( Δ N ) L , P 0 ℓ = e x 0 ℓ , ℓ ∈ { 1 , … , L } . P_{t}=(P_{t}^{1},\dots,P_{t}^{L})\in(\Delta_{N})^{L},\qquad P_{0}^{\ell}=e_{x_{0}^{\ell}},\quad\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}. (31) We then define the forward process independently across positions: p t | 0 ​ ( P t ∣ P 0 ) = ∏ ℓ = 1 L Dir ⁡ ( P t ℓ , β t ​ ( P 0 ℓ , π ) ) , β t ​ ( P 0 ℓ , π ) = c t ​ ( α t ​ P 0 ℓ + ( 1 − α t ) ​ π ) . p_{t\mid 0}(P_{t}\mid P_{0})=\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathrm{Dir}\bigl(P_{t}^{\ell};\beta_{t}(P_{0}^{\ell},\pi)\bigr),\qquad\beta_{t}(P_{0}^{\ell},\pi)=c_{t}\bigl(\alpha_{t}P_{0}^{\ell}+(1-\alpha_{t})\pi\bigr). (32) The denoiser is now a joint sequence model P ^ θ : ( Δ N ) L × [ 0 , 1 ] → ( Δ N ) L , P ^ θ ​ ( t , P t ) = ( P ^ 0 1 , … , P ^ 0 L ) , \hat{P}_{\theta}:(\Delta_{N})^{L}\times[0,1]\to(\Delta_{N})^{L},\qquad\hat{P}_{\theta}(t,P_{t})=(\hat{P}_{0}^{1},\dots,\hat{P}_{0}^{L}), (33) where each P ^ 0 ℓ ∈ Δ N \hat{P}_{0}^{\ell}\in\Delta_{N} is the predicted clean distribution at position ℓ \ell . Importantly, although the forward and reverse kernels factorize across positions, each P ^ 0 ℓ \hat{P}_{0}^{\ell} can depend on the full noisy sequence P t P_{t} . Training is performed with the sequence-level extension of the cross-entropy objective. At inference time, Section 3.1 is applied independently at each position after sampling a clean token from each predicted categorical distribution. More precisely, for any 0 < s < t ≤ 1 0<s<t\leq 1 , we first draw, conditionally independently across positions, x ~ 0 ℓ ∼ Cat ⁡ ( P ^ 0 ℓ ) , P ~ 0 ℓ = e x ~ 0 ℓ , ℓ ∈ { 1 , … , L } . \widetilde{x}_{0}^{\ell}\sim\mathrm{Cat}(\hat{P}_{0}^{\ell}),\qquad\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\ell}=e_{\widetilde{x}_{0}^{\ell}},\qquad\ell\in\{1,\dots,L\}. sections.heading: Appendix D Fast Sampling of Dirichlet Random Variables
sections.text: In order to sample from Dirichlet distribution efficiently one leverage the representation of Dirichlet distributions in terms of Gamma distributions. More precisely, for Y ∼ Dir ⁡ ( α ) Y\sim\mathrm{Dir}(\alpha) with α = ( α 1 , … , α N ) \alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{N}) can be efficiently obtained by defining Y = ( X 1 ∑ j = 1 N X j , … , X N ∑ j = 1 N X j ) , Y=\left(\frac{X_{1}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}X_{j}},\dots,\frac{X_{N}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N}X_{j}}\right), (44) with X i ∼ Gamma ⁡ ( α i , 1 ) X_{i}\sim\mathrm{Gamma}(\alpha_{i},1) . Hence in order to sample efficiently from a Dirichlet distribution one must efficiently sample from a Gamma \mathrm{Gamma} distribution. In order to do so, we leverage the Marsaglia–Tsang algorithm, Marsaglia & Tsang (2000) ; see also Algorithm 3 . However, the current implementation of the Gamma sampler in Jax is either slow or approximate Bradbury et al. (2018) , see https://github.com/jax-ml/jax/issues/38141 . In order to generate a Gamma \mathrm{Gamma} random variable of shape ( d 1 , … , d n ) (d_{1},\dots,d_{n}) , the current official implementation splits an original key d = ∏ i = 1 n d i d=\prod_{i=1}^{n}d_{i} times. Then it proceeds in using vmap on those d d dimensions. The body of this parallelised function also contains key splitting. This incurs large memory overhead which makes the whole function slow. Instead, we propose an exact implementation which does not rely on vmap and therefore do not require creating many keys which significantly reduce the memory overhead. We reproduce a minimal example of this overhead as well as our solution below and provide some performance benchmark on CPU hardware, see Figure 4 . All benchmarks were conducted on an AMD EPYC 7B13 processor (32 physical cores, 2.45GHz base clock, 128MB L3 cache) with 117 GB of DDR4 RAM using Jax and the XLA CPU backend in single precision ( float32 ). Finally, we highlight that a recent approach by Greaves (2026) show that Gamma \mathrm{Gamma} distributions can be generated as extended one-liner, thereby resolving a conjecture of Devroye (1996) . In practice, the approach leverages a Generalized Acceptance-Complement procedure with a Gaussian proposal and a triangular symmetric complement. In particular, the proposed sampler only requires three draws of independent random variables. As a consequence, this new sampler i) decreases drastically the number of calls to pseudo random number generators ii) bypasses the need of a while loop to sample from the distribution. Early benchmarks of this approach forecast a sampling speed-up of 1.5x over our fast implementation of the Marsaglia–Tsang algorithm. sections.heading: Algorithm and Links with Literature.
sections.text: Leveraging the loss given in Section G.1 , we consider an algorithm to learn a distilled model. The full algorithm is given in Algorithm 4 . With exact conditional means, i.e., the denoisers are exact, and a valid pathwise derivative of the corruption map, Algorithm 4 is valid. In practice, learned denoisers approximate these conditional means, yielding an approximate gradient. To differentiate through the forward process, we here differentiate through the fast Gamma \mathrm{Gamma} implementation of Appendix D . Note that one might be able to leverage the implementation of Greaves (2026) to obtain numerical gradients which are more precise. We leave this exploration for future work. It is apparent that Algorithm 4 follows the same pattern as many existing distillation algorithms such as DMD ( Yin et al., 2024 ) but also Multistep Moment matching Distillation (MMD) ( Salimans et al., 2024 ) . In fact, our algorithm can be interpreted as a simplicial extension of the MMD algorithm. In both cases, we train a generator network G η G_{\eta} as well as an auxiliary denoiser approximating 𝔼 ℙ 0 | t η , s ​ [ P 0 s | P t ] \mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{0|t}^{\eta,s}}[P_{0}^{s}|P_{t}] . Another line of related work is Universal Distillation Matching (UDM) and its discrete counterpart Inverse Distillation Language Model (IDLM) ( Kornilov et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . While closely related to our method, we highlight the key differences between these methods and our contribution in Section G.2 . sections.heading: G.2 Link with Inverse Distilled Language Models
sections.text: In this section, we draw connections between the Simplex DMD framework and the Inverse Distilled Language Model (IDLM) approach ( Kornilov et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . We show that both methods share a common structure but differ in how the gradient of the generative loss is handled, with the Simplex DMD framework resolving a fundamental difficulty encountered in IDLM.

sections.heading: H.1 General overview
sections.text: In this section, we present an overview of simplex diffusion models and their applications to discrete data generation. For Discrete Diffusions, we refer the reader to the original paper of Austin et al. (2021) and more recent extensions ( Campbell et al., 2022 ; Benton et al., 2024 ; Lou et al., 2024 ; Sahoo et al., 2024 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . Several simplex diffusion models are obtained by defining a forward stochastic process directly on the simplex. Then, relying on tools from time-reversal ( Haussmann & Pardoux, 1986 ) , similar to Song et al. (2021b) in Euclidean state spaces, one can define a generative process. In Richemond et al. (2022) , inspired by Baker et al. (2018) , the forward process corresponds to a set of N N Cox–Ingersoll–Ross processes that converge to a Gamma distribution and to a Dirichlet distribution after renormalization. Floto et al. (2023) consider another forward process based on a softmax transformation of an Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. One of the main advantages of Floto et al. (2023) is that for any t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] the distribution p t | 0 p_{t|0} is a logistic normal distribution which is easy to sample. Dirichlet Diffusion Score Models (DDSMs) ( Avdeyev et al., 2023 ) consider instead a Jacobi diffusion process as a forward process that converges to a Beta \mathrm{Beta} distribution. By then leveraging a stick-breaking construction, the authors obtain a forward process converging to a Dirichlet distribution. Benton et al. (2024) instead use the Wright-Fisher diffusion as a forward process, a diffusion on the simplex originating from genetics. Recently, in Chandra et al. (2026) , it was shown that discrete, continuous and Wright-Fisher diffusions could arise from a similar particle perspective, where the Wright-Fisher diffusion is obtained as a limit where the number of particles goes to infinity and we consider reproduction within the particles’ evolution. Yet another approach is to define diffusion models taking into account the special geometry of the simplex. Doing so, it is then possible to define diffusion models on an associated statistical manifold using general techniques from Flow Matching and Riemannian diffusion models ( De Bortoli et al., 2022 ; Huang et al., 2022 ; Chen & Lipman, 2024 ) . While in Cheng et al. (2024) ; Davis et al. (2024) ; Williams et al. (2026) , the authors derive the metrics on the simplex using the Fisher–Rao connection, Boll et al. (2024) ; Boll et al. (2025) consider e e -connections, see ( Davis et al., 2024 , Appendix E.2) for a discussion of the choice of metrics. In Han et al. (2023) ; Mahabadi et al. (2024) ; Jo & Hwang (2025) , the authors consider a Gaussian diffusion in the space of logits embeddings. Those different approaches, along with the one ignoring the geometry of the simplex and simply performing a linear diffusion in that space ( Dunn & Koes, 2024 ) , can be unified using the concept of α \alpha -divergence to define the statistical manifold (see Cheng et al., 2025 ). Another approach incorporating the geometry of the simplex into the generation process is to consider a constrained forward process using either projection or reflection of the original Stochastic Differential Equation ( Liu et al., 2023b ; Fishman et al., 2024 ; Fishman et al., 2023 ; Lou & Ermon, 2023 ) . The closest work to ours is the Dirichlet Flow Matching approach introduced by Stark et al. (2024) . In this work, the authors introduced a forward process akin to ours. The main difference between the two approaches arises from inference. While Stark et al. (2024) leverage a flow perspective, our approach is akin to DDIM ( Song et al., 2021a ) . We also provide a different temperature-parameterized process. Note that very recently Boget & Kalousis (2026) have proposed the same forward process as Stark et al. (2024) . They introduce an inference procedure which, like ours, allows for stochasticity but assumes p s | 0 , t ​ ( P s | P 0 , P t ) = p s | 0 ​ ( P s | P 0 ) p_{s|0,t}(P_{s}|P_{0},P_{t})=p_{s|0}(P_{s}|P_{0}) as in star-shaped diffusion models ( Okhotin et al., 2023 ) (corresponding to κ = 1 \kappa=1 in our case). Another concurrent work (Simplax) ( Sakurai et al., 2026 ) also uses Dirichlet simplex states, but their denoiser and sampling procedure operate on categorical samples rather than the continuous simplex state itself. We conclude by mentioning that Haviv et al. (2025) introduce Wasserstein Flow Matching, i.e., define Flow Matching on the space of distributions, similar to the simplicial approach lifting distributions on a given state space to the space of distributions of distributions. Finally, we note that the recent work of Song et al. (2025) introducing Shortlisting Models (SLMs) also claims a simplex approach as they “aim to preserve the core principle of simplex-based methods, gradual information growth ”. To do so, they operate on the space of probability vectors. Starting from a single full probability vector, they progressively eliminate categories until the final denoised state is one-hot.

sections.heading: H.2 Simplex Relaxation for Discrete Diffusion
sections.text: In this section, we describe the approach of Sakurai et al. (2026) and compare it with our framework. We first outline how they construct their forward process alongside their simplex relaxation. Next, we discuss their chosen training loss. Finally, we investigate their sampling procedure and show that it can be simplified to bypass the simplex relaxation, thereby highlighting a fundamental difference from Simplex Diffusion Models.

sections.heading: I.1 Discrete Diffusion Models
sections.text: In this section, we outline the training and sampling procedures for Discrete Diffusion models. For simplicity, we describe processes over scalar variables, and the extension to sequences is similar to Section C.1 . Refer to Austin et al. (2021) ; Campbell et al. (2022) ; Sahoo et al. (2024) ; Shi et al. (2024) ; Schiff et al. (2025) ; von Rütte et al. (2025) ; Gourevitch et al. (2026) for the derivations. Discrete Diffusion Models define a corruption process ( 2 ) in terms of a prior π ∈ Δ N \pi\in\Delta_{N} . Prior work mainly focuses on the absorbing (or masked) prior π mask = m \pi^{\text{mask}}=m , where m m is the one-hot embedding of a special [ mask ] token, and the uniform prior π unif = 𝟏 / N \pi^{\text{unif}}=\mathbf{1}/N . Several works study mixtures of π mask \pi^{\text{mask}} and π unif \pi^{\text{unif}} ( Fathi et al., 2025 ; von Rütte et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) , or data-dependent priors ( Alamdari et al., 2023 ; Vignac et al., 2023 ; Qin et al., 2025 ) but it is not clear whether elaborate priors are necessary at scale for language modeling ( Sahoo et al., 2026 ; von Rütte et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: Sampling.

sections.heading: Temperature.
sections.text: All samplers can scale the logits ζ \zeta of the denoiser by a temperature T > 0 T>0 , i.e., they use the prediction softmax ⁡ ( ζ / T ) \mathrm{softmax}(\zeta/T) (148) instead of softmax ⁡ ( ζ ) \mathrm{softmax}(\zeta) . T = 1 T=1 recovers the denoiser prediction, and T → 0 T\to 0 approaches greedy decoding. For SDMs, the scaled prediction replaces P ^ θ ​ ( t , P t ) \hat{P}_{\theta}(t,P_{t}) in the transition of Section 3.1 .

sections.heading: Training.
I.2 Predictor-Corrector Sampler
sections.text: Our PC baselines for MDMs and UDMs use a pure predict-and-renoise sampler. Instead of the ancestral transition p ^ s | t θ \hat{p}^{\theta}_{s|t} , each step (1) samples x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} from the plug-in posterior at target time 0 0 , i.e., the bridge ( 144 ) with s = 0 s=0 and e x 0 e_{x_{0}} replaced by the denoiser prediction, and (2) re-applies the forward process ( 2 ) to x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} at the next time. Let ( t i ) i = 0 n (t_{i})_{i=0}^{n} be the sampling time grid ( Section J.1 ), and let 𝐱 θ ​ ( t , x t ) \mathbf{x}_{\theta}(t,x_{t}) denote the denoiser, with logits scaled by the temperature T T of ( 148 ). Starting from x t n ∼ Cat ⁡ ( π ) x_{t_{n}}\sim\operatorname{Cat}(\pi) , we repeat for i = n , … , 1 i=n,\dots,1 : (Predict) x ^ 0 ∼ Cat ⁡ ( 𝐱 θ ​ ( t i , x t i ) ) , \displaystyle\hat{x}_{0}\sim\operatorname{Cat}\bigl(\mathbf{x}_{\theta}(t_{i},x_{t_{i}})\bigr), (152) (Re-noise) x t i − 1 ∼ p t i − 1 | 0 ( ⋅ ∣ x ^ 0 ) = Cat ( α t i − 1 e x ^ 0 + ( 1 − α t i − 1 ) π ) , \displaystyle x_{t_{i-1}}\sim p_{t_{i-1}|0}(\cdot\mid\hat{x}_{0})=\operatorname{Cat}\bigl(\alpha_{t_{i-1}}e_{\hat{x}_{0}}+(1-\alpha_{t_{i-1}})\pi\bigr), (153) independently for each position, and we return x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} at the last step ( t 0 = 0 t_{0}=0 , α t 0 = 1 \alpha_{t_{0}}=1 ). The sampler therefore uses the bridge p s | 0 , t ​ ( x s ∣ x 0 , x t ) = p s | 0 ​ ( x s ∣ x 0 ) p_{s|0,t}(x_{s}\mid x_{0},x_{t})=p_{s|0}(x_{s}\mid x_{0}) with the plug-in prediction, as in star-shaped diffusion ( Okhotin et al., 2023 ) . Every step discards x t i x_{t_{i}} except through the prediction x ^ 0 \hat{x}_{0} . For MDMs, this means that tokens unmasked at earlier steps can be masked again, which lets the sampler revise earlier choices.

sections.heading: I.3 Self-Conditioning and Loopholing
sections.text: Because Discrete Diffusion models operate directly on discrete state spaces, the rich categorical distribution predicted by the denoiser collapses into a single discrete token value at each sampling step. Consequently, sampling discards the uncertainty of the denoiser. Therefore, it is common to resort to Self-Conditioning (SC; Chen et al., 2022 ) or Loopholing ( Jo et al., 2026 ) to propagate continuous information across sampling steps. We implement SC following Jo et al. (2026) .

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: We decompose the denoiser into three parts. An embedding layer e ⁡ ( ⋅ ) e(\cdot) maps the input state x t x_{t} to one vector per position. A backbone f θ f_{\theta} maps the embedded input and the time t t to the last hidden representation h h , which we call the latent. An output head g g (a linear projection followed by a softmax) maps h h to the predicted distribution over clean tokens. Without SC, the denoiser computes h = f θ ​ ( e ⁡ ( x t ) , t ) , 𝐱 θ ​ ( t , x t ) = g ⁡ ( h ) . h=f_{\theta}\bigl(e(x_{t}),t\bigr),\qquad\mathbf{x}_{\theta}(t,x_{t})=g(h). (154) With SC, the denoiser additionally receives a latent h prev h^{\text{prev}} and adds it to the input embedding after a LayerNorm LN ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{LN}(\cdot) : h = f θ ​ ( e ⁡ ( x t ) + LN ⁡ ( h prev ) , t ) , 𝐱 θ ​ ( t , x t , h prev ) = g ⁡ ( h ) . h=f_{\theta}\bigl(e(x_{t})+\mathrm{LN}(h^{\text{prev}}),t\bigr),\qquad\mathbf{x}_{\theta}(t,x_{t},h^{\text{prev}})=g(h). (155) Setting h prev = 0 h^{\text{prev}}=0 recovers a denoiser without context. Following Jo et al. (2026) , we initialize the scale and shift of LN \mathrm{LN} to zero, so that SC initially leaves the input unchanged.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: Let sg ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathrm{sg}(\cdot) denote the stop-gradient operator, which acts as the identity in the forward pass and blocks gradients in the backward pass. With probability p SC = 0.9 p_{\text{SC}}=0.9 , we apply SC: a first forward pass with h prev = 0 h^{\text{prev}}=0 and without gradient produces a latent h 0 h^{0} , and a second forward pass ( 155 ) with h prev = sg ⁡ ( h 0 ) h^{\text{prev}}=\mathrm{sg}(h^{0}) produces the prediction on which we compute the loss. With probability 1 − p SC 1-p_{\text{SC}} , we use a single forward pass with h prev = 0 h^{\text{prev}}=0 . This avoids unrolling the sampling trajectory during training.

sections.heading: Matching the Training FLOPs.
sections.text: We count the cost of a forward pass as 1 1 and that of a forward and backward pass as 3 3 . A training step with SC then costs on average 3 + p SC ⋅ 1 = 3 + 0.9 = 3.9 3+p_{\text{SC}}\cdot 1=3+0.9=3.9 forward-equivalents, against 3 3 without SC. To match the training FLOPs of models trained without SC, we train SC models for a fraction 3 / 3.9 ≈ 0.77 3/3.9\approx 0.77 of the training steps.

sections.heading: Sampling.
sections.text: At the first sampling step, h prev = 0 h^{\text{prev}}=0 . The latent h h computed at step t i t_{i} is then passed as h prev h^{\text{prev}} to step t i − 1 t_{i-1} . Next to the sampled discrete state, each step thus carries a deterministic continuous state. This adds one LayerNorm and one addition per step, and no extra forward pass.

sections.heading: I.4 Dirichlet Flow Matching
sections.text: This section contains additional background on Euclidean and Dirichlet Flow Matching. To ensure consistency with the Discrete Diffusion literature, we denote the noise distribution by p 1 p_{1} and the empirical data distribution by p 0 p_{0} .

sections.heading: Continuous Normalizing Flows.
sections.text: Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs; Chen et al., 2018 ; Grathwohl et al., 2018 ) are generative models on ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} that transport samples from a tractable prior p 1 = p noise p_{1}=p_{\text{noise}} to an unknown data distribution p 0 = p data p_{0}=p_{\text{data}} . To match the rest of the paper, we reverse the usual CNF time convention, in which t = 0 t=0 is noise. The time-dependent velocity field u t θ : ℝ d → ℝ d u_{t}^{\theta}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} induces a flow map ϕ t : ℝ d → ℝ d \phi_{t}\colon\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} via the Ordinary Differential Equation (ODE): d ​ x t d ​ t = u t θ ​ ( x t ) , x 1 ∼ p 1 , \frac{\mathrm{d}x_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}=u_{t}^{\theta}(x_{t}),\quad x_{1}\sim p_{1}, (156) where θ \theta parameterizes a neural network. Integrating ( 156 ) from t = 1 t=1 to t = 0 t=0 maps approximately noise x 1 x_{1} to data x 0 = ϕ 0 ​ ( x 1 ) x_{0}=\phi_{0}(x_{1}) , defining intermediate densities p t = [ ϕ t ] ♯ ​ p 1 p_{t}=[\phi_{t}]_{\sharp}p_{1} along the probability path { p t } t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \{p_{t}\}_{t\in[0,1]} .

sections.text: Rather than leaving the velocity field u t θ u_{t}^{\theta} unconstrained and optimizing θ \theta through expensive ODE simulation, Flow Matching (FM) constructs a generative process using conditional probability paths p t | 0 ​ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) p_{t|0}(x_{t}\mid x_{0}) and conditional velocity fields u t | 0 ​ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) u_{t|0}(x_{t}\mid x_{0}) , conditioned on clean data samples x 0 ∼ p 0 x_{0}\sim p_{0} . From this conditional pair, we define p t ​ ( x t ) = ∫ p t | 0 ​ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) ​ p 0 ​ ( x 0 ) ​ d ​ x 0 . p_{t}(x_{t})=\int p_{t|0}(x_{t}\mid x_{0})\,p_{0}(x_{0})\,\mathrm{d}x_{0}. (157) and u t ​ ( x t ) = ∫ u t ​ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) ​ p 0 | t ​ ( x 0 ∣ x t ) ​ d ​ x 0 = ∫ u t ​ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) ​ p t | 0 ​ ( x t ∣ x 0 ) ​ p 0 ​ ( x 0 ) p t ​ ( x t ) ​ d ​ x 0 . u_{t}(x_{t})=\int u_{t}(x_{t}\mid x_{0})\,p_{0|t}(x_{0}\mid x_{t})\,\mathrm{d}x_{0}=\int u_{t}(x_{t}\mid x_{0})\frac{p_{t|0}(x_{t}\mid x_{0})p_{0}(x_{0})}{p_{t}(x_{t})}dx_{0}. (158) It can then be shown that these quantities (see e.g., Lipman et al. (2023) ) satisfy ∂ p t ​ ( x ) ∂ t + ∇ ⋅ ( p t ​ ( x ) ​ u t ​ ( x ) ) = 0 . \frac{\partial p_{t}(x)}{\partial t}+\nabla\cdot\big(p_{t}(x)u_{t}(x)\big)=0. (159) Satisfying ( 159 ) ensures that integrating an ODE of drift u t u_{t} from t = 1 t=1 to t = t ′ t=t^{\prime} produces a sample x t ′ ∼ p t ′ x_{t^{\prime}}\sim p_{t^{\prime}} .

sections.heading: Extension to the Simplex.
sections.text: Dirichlet Flow Matching (DFM; Stark et al., 2024 ) extends FM to the simplex Δ N \Delta_{N} to model categorical data. In particular, DFM tackles the issue of contracting support on Δ N \Delta_{N} by defining conditional probability paths with full support: p t | 0 ​ ( P t | P 0 ) = Dir ⁡ ( P t , 𝟏 + h t ​ P 0 ) . p_{t|0}(P_{t}|P_{0})=\mathrm{Dir}\big(P_{t};\mathbf{1}+h_{t}P_{0}\big). (160) Stark et al. (2024) show that when paired with the following conditional velocity field u t | 0 u_{t|0} , ( p t | 0 , u t | 0 ) (p_{t|0},u_{t|0}) satisfy the continuity equation. For P 0 P_{0} the one-hot embedding e i e_{i} of category i i , u t | 0 ​ ( P t | P 0 ) = C ⁡ ( P t , i , t ) ​ ( e i − P t ) , \displaystyle u_{t|0}(P_{t}|P_{0})=C(P_{t,i},t)(e_{i}-P_{t}), (161) C ⁡ ( P t , i , t ) = − I ~ P t , i ​ ( t + 1 , N − 1 ) ​ ℬ ⁡ ( t + 1 , N − 1 ) ( 1 − P t , i ) N − 1 ​ P t , i t , \displaystyle C(P_{t,i},t)=-\tilde{I}_{P_{t,i}}(t+1,N-1)\frac{\mathcal{B}(t+1,N-1)}{(1-P_{t,i})^{N-1}P^{t}_{t,i}}, where ℬ \mathcal{B} denotes the beta function, I ~ x ​ ( a , b ) = ∂ ∂ a ​ I x ​ ( a , b ) \tilde{I}_{x}(a,b)=\frac{\partial}{\partial a}I_{x}(a,b) the partial derivative of the regularized incomplete beta function, and N N the number of categories. Like us, Stark et al. (2024) train a denoiser p 0 | t θ ​ ( x 0 | x t ) : ( Δ N ) L ↦ ( Δ N ) L p^{\theta}_{0|t}(x_{0}|x_{t}):(\Delta_{N})^{L}\mapsto(\Delta_{N})^{L} with Cross-Entropy. However, their sampling dynamics differs, as they marginalize the conditional as in ( 158 ), replacing the true posterior by the learned one. Therefore Stark et al. (2024) propose a deterministic sampler, while ours is not, even in the case κ = 0 \kappa=0 ( Section 3 ). Part IV: Experimental Setup, Ablations and Results

sections.heading: J.1 Time Samplers and Sampling Schedules
sections.text: We distinguish two choices. The time sampler is the distribution of t t during training: uniform ( † ) or adaptive ( ‡ ). The sampling schedule is the time grid used at inference: linear, cosine or adaptive. The two can be combined freely, except that the adaptive schedule requires the adaptive time sampler, since it reuses the loss profile fitted during training.

sections.heading: Motivation.
sections.text: By default, recent Discrete Diffusion draws the time t t uniformly from t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] during training. However, recent continuous diffusion language models require adaptive time samplers ( Dieleman et al., 2022 ; Pynadath et al., 2026a ; Batzolis et al., 2026 ; Chemseddine et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ; Deschenaux & Gulcehre, 2026 ; Lee et al., 2026 ; Potaptchik et al., 2026 ; Raya et al., 2026 ; Roos et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) to perform well. During training, we use the derivative of the loss profile t ↦ d d ​ t ​ L t t\mapsto\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}L_{t} as a proxy for where the network learns the most. Assuming that the true loss increases monotonically with t t , the derivative d ​ L t d ​ t ≥ 0 \frac{\mathrm{d}{L_{t}}}{\mathrm{d}t}\geq 0 directly defines an importance density q ⁡ ( t ) ∝ d ​ L t d ​ t q(t)\propto\frac{\mathrm{d}{L_{t}}}{\mathrm{d}t} .

sections.heading: High-Level Algorithm.
sections.text: We maintain a ring buffer to store recent ( t , L t ) (t,L_{t}) pairs. During the first 1k training steps, we start with t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) to fill the buffer. Afterwards, every 50 50 training steps, we approximate the loss profile using the content of the ring buffer, with either B-splines ( Cox, 1972 ; de Boor, 1972 ) or with the mean per bucket, and differentiate via finite differences to obtain the empirical density q ^ ​ ( t ) ∝ d ​ L t d ​ t \hat{q}(t)\propto\frac{\mathrm{d}L_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t} . We track an EMA q ^ EMA \hat{q}_{\text{EMA}} of the successive densities q ^ \hat{q} with momentum 0.9 0.9 for stability. Let F ^ EMA \hat{F}_{\text{EMA}} denote the CDF obtained by numerically integrating q ^ EMA \hat{q}_{\text{EMA}} . Finally, we evaluate F ^ EMA \hat{F}_{\text{EMA}} on a fine grid of 1k values and store ( F ^ EMA ​ ( t ) , t ) (\hat{F}_{\text{EMA}}(t),t) . We evaluate t = F ^ EMA − 1 ​ ( u ) t=\hat{F}^{-1}_{\text{EMA}}(u) with linear interpolation for u ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) u\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) during training (inverse transform sampling).

sections.heading: Estimating the Loss Profile.
sections.text: Deschenaux & Gulcehre (2026) estimates L t L_{t} by fitting a global cubic B-spline with ridge regression. In preliminary experiments, we found that a simpler bucketed piecewise-linear estimator led to stronger performance. Therefore, we partition [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] into B = 50 B=50 uniform bins, compute the mean loss within each bin independently, and linearly interpolate, placing the estimated means at the center of each bin. We compute the density as q ^ ​ ( t ) = max ⁡ ( 0 , d ​ L d ​ t ) \hat{q}(t)=\max\left(0,\frac{\mathrm{d}L}{\mathrm{d}t}\right) . While the true d ​ L d ​ t \frac{\mathrm{d}L}{\mathrm{d}t} should be non-negative in principle, max \max removes numerical artifacts that would make the density negative.

sections.heading: Sampling Time Schedules.
sections.text: We define the sampling time grid as 0 = t 0 < t 1 < ⋯ < t n = 1 0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\dots<t_{n}=1 and compare three schedules. The first is the linear grid t i = i n t_{i}=\frac{i}{n} . The second is the cosine grid t i = cos ⁡ ( π 2 ​ ( 1 − i n ) ) t_{i}=\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\left(1-\frac{i}{n}\right)\right) ( Chang et al., 2022 ; Shi et al., 2024 ) . The third is an adaptive grid that reuses the loss profile fitted during training. Specifically, we take the final CDF F ^ EMA \hat{F}_{\text{EMA}} of the adaptive time sampler, stored as a lookup table of 1k points, and place the grid at uniform quantiles: t i = F ^ EMA − 1 ( i n ) , i = 0 , … , n , t_{i}=\hat{F}^{-1}_{\text{EMA}}\!\left(\tfrac{i}{n}\right),\qquad i=0,\dots,n, (162) evaluated by linear interpolation, exactly as during training. Since q ^ EMA ∝ max ⁡ ( 0 , d ​ L t d ​ t ) \hat{q}_{\text{EMA}}\propto\max(0,\frac{\mathrm{d}L_{t}}{\mathrm{d}t}) , the grid spends more denoising steps on the noise levels where the loss changes fastest. These are the same noise levels at which the adaptive sampler concentrates training. The grid needs no extra computation or tuning at inference.

sections.heading: J.2 Denoiser Input for SDMs
sections.text: The SDM denoiser receives a sequence of simplex states P t = ( P t 1 , … , P t L ) ∈ ( Δ N ) L P_{t}=(P_{t}^{1},\dots,P_{t}^{L})\in(\Delta_{N})^{L} ( Section C.1 ). As in Section I.3 , an embedding layer e e maps the input to one vector in ℝ d \mathbb{R}^{d} per position, a backbone f θ f_{\theta} maps the embedded sequence and the time t t to the last hidden representation h h , and an output head g g maps h h to the predicted distribution P ^ θ ​ ( t , P t ) \hat{P}_{\theta}(t,P_{t}) . Let E ∈ ℝ N × d E\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} be the input embedding matrix, whose i i -th row E i E_{i} embeds token i ∈ 𝒳 i\in\mathcal{X} . We consider two embeddings of P t P_{t} , each with or without Self-Conditioning.

sections.heading: Expectation.
sections.text: We feed the expected embedding e ​ ( P t ) ℓ = ( P t ℓ ) ⊤ ​ E = ∑ i = 1 N P t , i ℓ ​ E i = 𝔼 X ∼ Cat ⁡ ( P t ℓ ) ​ [ E X ] . e(P_{t})^{\ell}=(P_{t}^{\ell})^{\top}E=\sum\nolimits_{i=1}^{N}P_{t,i}^{\ell}\,E_{i}=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mathrm{Cat}(P_{t}^{\ell})}\bigl[E_{X}\bigr]. (163) This input uses the full belief state: two states with the same most likely token but different uncertainty can map to different inputs. Note that we are not ensured that we do not necessarily have that e ⁡ ( P ) = e ⁡ ( Q ) e(P)=e(Q) implies P = Q P=Q , i.e. the embedding is not necessarily injective. Since P t ℓ P_{t}^{\ell} has strictly positive entries almost surely, ( 163 ) requires a dense product with E E , which costs 2 ​ N ​ d 2Nd FLOPs per token, as much as the output projection. On TinyGSM ( N ≈ 49 N\approx 49 k, d = 768 d=768 ), this adds ≈ 29 % \approx 29\% to the FLOPs of a forward pass of our 12-layer DiT.

sections.heading: Argmax.
sections.text: To avoid this product, we embed only the most likely token, both during training and at sampling: e ​ ( P t ) ℓ = E x ^ t ℓ , x ^ t ℓ = argmax i ​ P t , i ℓ , e(P_{t})^{\ell}=E_{\hat{x}_{t}^{\ell}},\qquad\hat{x}_{t}^{\ell}=\mathrm{argmax}_{i}P_{t,i}^{\ell}, (164) which is a table lookup, as for MDMs and UDMs. The denoiser then sees only x ^ t ℓ \hat{x}_{t}^{\ell} , but the sampler is unchanged: the transition of Section 3.1 still acts on the full state P t P_{t} , so the belief state is still carried from step to step.

sections.heading: Self-Conditioning.
sections.text: We also combine both inputs with SC, as described in Section I.3 , with the simplex state P t P_{t} in place of x t x_{t} : the backbone receives e ⁡ ( P t ) + LN ⁡ ( h prev ) e(P_{t})+\mathrm{LN}(h^{\text{prev}}) . SC gives the denoiser a rich summary of its previous prediction, which complements the argmax input in particular (Argmax + SC).

sections.heading: Which Input Is Used Where.
sections.text: On Sudoku, SDMs use the expectation input, with and without SC ( Table 1 ). On TinyGSM, we report the expectation, Argmax and Argmax + SC inputs ( Tables 29 , 30 , 31 and 32 ).

sections.heading: J.3 Dirichlet Flow Matching Baseline
sections.text: To understand the benefits of our simplex based method, we also compared to the Dirichlet Flow Matching (DFM) method, as described in Section I.4 . The original implementation provided by the authors at https://github.com/HannesStark/dirichlet-flow-matching does not include the ability to run on any of the datasets we experimented on. Furthermore, the original implementation and experiments deal with small vocab sizes (only up to 160 categories) whereas our text experiments use up to 50k tokens. We therefore re-implemented and extended the DFM method to provide a fair comparison to our approach. We made two key changes to DFM. The first was to use the adaptive time sampler during training which we found helped performance on TinyGSM for our method. In the original presentation in Stark et al. (2024) , eq (14) presents the corruption distribution as (in the authors’ original notation) p t ​ ( 𝐱 | 𝐱 1 = 𝐞 i ) = Dir ​ ( 𝐱 , α = 𝟏 + t ⋅ 𝐞 i ) . p_{t}(\mathbf{x}|\mathbf{x}_{1}=\mathbf{e}_{i})=\text{Dir}(\mathbf{x};\mathbf{\alpha}=\mathbf{1}+t\cdot\mathbf{e}_{i}). (165) In the original implementation during training, t t is sampled as an exponential random variable with scale parameter α scale \alpha_{\text{scale}} , t ∼ Exp ​ ( 1 α scale ) t\sim\text{Exp}(\frac{1}{\alpha_{\text{scale}}}) . We instead sample t t with the adaptive time sampler described in Section J.1 . Secondly, we improved the sampling implementation to handle much larger numbers of categories than the original implementation. Sampling in DFM requires integrating the conditional velocity field ( 161 ) towards target vertices e i e_{i} on the simplex Δ N \Delta_{N} . sections.heading: Data Generation.
sections.text: We generate 9x9 Sudoku puzzles with 30 visible cells using the backtracking generator of Alp (2024) . We produce partial grids by iteratively removing cells and verifying that the solution remains unique. We ensure that the training and validation sets share no full grids. We use 200k training and 5k validation puzzles (instead of the 48k/2k split in Deschenaux & Gulcehre (2026) ; Kim et al. (2026b) ) since we observed mild overfitting in preliminary experiments, especially when using the adaptive time sampler. We report the exact-match accuracy on the validation set.

sections.heading: Tokenization.
sections.text: We represent each puzzle as a sequence of 180 tokens drawn from a vocabulary of size 14. We map digits { 1 , … , 9 } \{1,\dots,9\} directly to their numerical values, empty cells _ to ID 0, row separators | to ID 10, sequence boundaries [ bos ] to ID 11, (unused) padding to ID 12, and the [ mask ] to ID 13. To accommodate both autoregressive and diffusion algorithms, we concatenate the unsolved puzzle and its complete solution into a sequence of 180 tokens: ( [ bos ] , 5 , 3 , _ , … , 2 , | , … , | , _ , … , 9 ⏟ Prompt / Unsolved Puzzle ​ ( 90 ​ tokens ) , [ bos ] , 5 , 3 , 4 , … , 2 , | , … , | , 3 , … , 9 ⏟ Target / Complete Solution ​ ( 90 ​ tokens ) ) . \Big(\underbrace{\text{\text{[{bos}]}},\,5,3,\texttt{\_},\dots,2,\,\texttt{|},\dots,\texttt{|},\,\texttt{\_},\dots,9}_{\text{Prompt / Unsolved Puzzle }(90\text{ tokens})},\;\underbrace{\text{\text{[{bos}]}},\,5,3,4,\dots,2,\,\texttt{|},\dots,\texttt{|},\,3,\dots,9}_{\text{Target / Complete Solution }(90\text{ tokens})}\Big). (173) During training, we only corrupt the target tokens and keep the first half clean as conditioning. During inference, we start from a clean prompt and denoise only the second half.

sections.heading: Architecture and Hyperparameters.
sections.text: We train an 8-layer Diffusion Transformer (DiT) ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) with hidden dimension 512, 8 attention heads, an MLP expansion ratio of 4, 1D Rotary Positional Embeddings ( Su et al., 2024 ) , and untied input/output embeddings (28.6M total parameters). We apply a 0.1 dropout rate to the output projection ( Sahoo et al., 2024 ) . We train with Adam ( β 1 = 0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 , ϵ = 10 − 8 \beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.999,\epsilon=10^{-8} ), gradient clipping at maximum norm 1.0 1.0 , and no weight decay. The learning rate warms up linearly to 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} over 2.5k steps and remains constant afterwards. We maintain an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the parameters with decay 0.9999 0.9999 for evaluation for all methods. We implement time conditioning via Adaptive LayerNorm (AdaLN) ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) . The time-independent variants (AR and absorbing diffusion) receive a constant (zero) vector in place of time-conditioning, to share the exact same architecture with the other approaches. We train for 50k steps with a global batch size of 256 in full 32-bit precision ( ≈ 77 % \approx 77\% of the steps, i.e. 38,462, for SC variants, to match the training FLOPs; Section I.3 ).

sections.heading: Tokenization.
sections.text: We train our models on TinyGSM ( Liu et al., 2023a ) , a dataset containing approximately 11.8M synthetic grade-school math word problems associated with executable Python programs producing the correct answer. We evaluate the models zero-shot on the 1319 test problems of GSM8K ( Cobbe et al., 2021 ) by executing a generated program and verifying its numerical output. Following Deschenaux & Gulcehre (2026) , we tokenize TinyGSM with the SmolLM tokenizer ( Allal et al., 2025 ) (49k tokens). Unlike GPT-2, SmolLM pretrains on code, and thus its tokenizer compresses Python programs better. Kim et al. (2026a) originally used the Qwen2 tokenizer ( Yang et al., 2024 ) , but its 151k tokens induce huge embedding tables, and therefore we chose SmolLM as a compact alternative.

sections.heading: Architecture and Hyperparameters.
sections.text: We train a 12-layer Diffusion Transformer (DiT) ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) with hidden dimension 768, 12 attention heads, an MLP expansion ratio of 4, 1D Rotary Positional Embeddings ( Su et al., 2024 ) , and untied input and output embeddings (167.9M total parameters). Following Sahoo et al. (2024) , we apply a 0.1 dropout rate to the output projection. We optimize all models using Adam ( Kingma & Ba, 2014 ) ( β 1 = 0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 , ϵ = 10 − 8 \beta_{1}=0.9,\beta_{2}=0.999,\epsilon=10^{-8} ) without weight decay, clipping gradient norms at 1.0 1.0 . We linearly warm up the learning rate to 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} over 2,500 steps and hold it constant thereafter. We maintain an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the parameters with decay 0.9999 0.9999 and evaluate the EMA weights across all methods, including the autoregressive baseline. We implement time conditioning via Adaptive LayerNorm (AdaLN) ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) with a conditioning dimension of 128. The time-independent models (autoregressive and absorbing Discrete Diffusion) receive a constant zero vector as time conditioning, to keep the architecture the same across experiments. We train each model for 250k steps with a global batch size of 512 in full 32-bit floating-point precision ( ≈ 77 % \approx 77\% of the steps for SC variants, to match the training FLOPs; Section I.3 ). We train all SDMs with the adaptive time sampler ( Section J.1 ). During evaluation, we run 512 sampling steps for all diffusion variants unless stated otherwise.

sections.heading: AST Diversity Score.
sections.text: We measure how structurally different the K = 5 K=5 programs sampled for each GSM8K problem are by comparing their abstract syntax trees (ASTs). For each sample, we keep the text from the first function definition onward (or the content of a Markdown code block, if present), parse it with Python’s ast module, and discard samples that do not parse. We then normalize each tree: we remove docstrings, rename user-defined variables, functions and arguments to canonical identifiers within each scope ( VAR0 , VAR1 , …) while keeping built-in names such as sum or range , and replace keyword-argument names and import aliases by fixed placeholders. Each node is labeled by its node type; names also carry their canonical identifier, constants their type and value, and arithmetic operators their type. For two normalized trees T a T_{a} and T b T_{b} with | T a | |T_{a}| and | T b | |T_{b}| nodes, we compute the tree edit distance TED ⁡ ( T a , T b ) \mathrm{TED}(T_{a},T_{b}) ( Zhang & Shasha, 1989 ) with unit costs for insertion, deletion and relabeling, and define the similarity sim ⁡ ( T a , T b ) = max ⁡ ( 0 , 1 − TED ⁡ ( T a , T b ) max ⁡ ( | T a | , | T b | ) ) ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] . \mathrm{sim}(T_{a},T_{b})=\max\Bigl(0,\,1-\frac{\mathrm{TED}(T_{a},T_{b})}{\max(|T_{a}|,|T_{b}|)}\Bigr)\in[0,1]. (174) For a problem i i whose set of parsable samples 𝒱 i \mathcal{V}_{i} has at least two elements, the diversity is one minus the mean pairwise similarity, D i = 1 − ( | 𝒱 i | 2 ) − 1 ​ ∑ a < b ∈ 𝒱 i sim ⁡ ( T a , T b ) . D_{i}=1-\binom{|\mathcal{V}_{i}|}{2}^{-1}\sum_{a<b\in\mathcal{V}_{i}}\mathrm{sim}(T_{a},T_{b}). (175) We report 100 ⋅ 1 | ℐ | ∑ i ∈ ℐ D i 100\cdot\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}D_{i} , where ℐ \mathcal{I} is the set of problems with at least two parsable samples; higher is more diverse. AST Div. (Correct) is the same score computed only on the samples whose execution returns the reference answer, averaged over the problems with at least two such samples. It measures whether a model finds structurally different correct solutions, rather than rewarding diversity that comes from incorrect programs.

sections.heading: Tokenization.
sections.text: We evaluate unconditional language modeling on OpenWebText (OWT) ( Gokaslan & Cohen, 2019 ) . Following prior work, we tokenize OWT using the GPT-2 tokenizer ( Radford et al., 2019 ) (50257 tokens) and pack documents into sequences of 1024 tokens. Unlike Sudoku and TinyGSM, which require conditional prefix completion, we corrupt all 1024 positions during training and denoise sequences from scratch during inference. We measure the sample quality with the Generative Perplexity (Gen. PPL) under a pretrained GPT-2-large model and the unigram entropy. Specifically, we produce Pareto curves, following Pynadath et al. (2026a) .

sections.heading: Architecture and Hyperparameters.
sections.text: We use the same 12-layer DiT architecture as in TinyGSM. We use the exact same optimizer, learning rate schedule, AdaLN time conditioning, EMA decay rate, and global batch size as well. To follow the academic literature, we train each model for 1M steps. We sample the diffusion models with 64 steps, and the AR model token by token (1024 steps).

sections.heading: J.7 Language Understanding
sections.text: We evaluate our model on language understanding benchmarks such as ARC-easy ( Clark et al., 2018 ) , PIQA ( Bisk et al., 2020 ) and HellaSwag ( Zellers et al., 2019 ) . The goal of this benchmark is to evaluate the accuracy of a language model to choose the correct continuation when faced with multiple choices for a given context prompt. This is a significant departure from the sample quality metrics that we report for Sudoku, TinyGSM and OWT. We compare our method to GPT-2 ( Radford et al., 2019 ) , the retrained LLaMA baseline ( Touvron et al., 2023 ) of von Rütte et al. (2025) , Generalized Interpolating Discrete Diffusion (GIDDs) ( von Rütte et al., 2025 ) , Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) as reported in Deschenaux & Gulcehre (2025) and Partition Generative Models (PGMs) ( Deschenaux et al., 2026b ) . In each scenario we are given a context s s of length L s L_{s} and possible continuations c ( 1 ) , … , c ( n ) c^{(1)},\dots,c^{(n)} ( n = 2 n=2 in the case of PIQA, and n = 4 n=4 in the case of ARC-easy and HellaSwag). For a continuation c = ( c 1 , … , c L c ) c=(c^{1},\dots,c^{L_{c}}) of length L c L_{c} , we denote by x = ( s , c ) ∈ 𝒳 L x=(s,c)\in\mathcal{X}^{L} the full sequence, with L = L s + L c L=L_{s}+L_{c} . For AR models, the score of a continuation is given by S AR ​ ( s , c ) = ∑ ℓ = 1 L c log ⁡ p θ ​ ( c ℓ ∣ s , c 1 , … , c ℓ − 1 ) . S_{\text{AR}}(s,c)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L_{c}}\log p_{\theta}(c^{\ell}\mid s,c^{1},\dots,c^{\ell-1}). (176) In the case of MDMs, the score is given by S MDM ( s , c ) = − ∑ ℓ = 1 L ∫ 0 1 α t ′ 1 − α t ⟨ x ℓ , log 𝐱 θ ( t , x t ) ℓ ⟩ d t . S_{\text{MDM}}(s,c)=-\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\alpha_{t}^{\prime}}{1-\alpha_{t}}\langle x^{\ell},\log\mathbf{x}_{\theta}(t,x_{t})^{\ell}\rangle\mathrm{d}t. (177) In von Rütte et al. (2025) , the integral is discretized on a uniform grid with 128 NFE, whereas in Deschenaux & Gulcehre (2025) ; Deschenaux et al. (2026b) the authors sample uniformly 1024 1024 times in the interval [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . In our case, the noising process retains significant information about the initial sample contrary to MDMs. Therefore, we consider an additional regularization term emphasizing that we care about the continuation and not only the whole text plausibility. In practice, we consider S SDM ​ ( s , c ) = ∑ ℓ = L s + 1 L ∫ 0 1 q t ​ ⟨ x ℓ , log ⁡ x θ ​ ( t , x t ) ℓ ⟩ ​ 𝑑 t − w ​ ∑ ℓ = L s + 1 L ∫ 0 1 q t ​ ⟨ x ~ ℓ , log ⁡ x θ ​ ( t , x ~ t ) ℓ ⟩ ​ 𝑑 t , S_{\text{SDM}}(s,c)=\sum_{\ell=L_{s}+1}^{L}\int_{0}^{1}q_{t}\langle x^{\ell},\log x_{\theta}(t,x_{t})^{\ell}\rangle\mathrm{d}t-w\sum_{\ell=L_{s}+1}^{L}\int_{0}^{1}q_{t}\langle\tilde{x}^{\ell},\log x_{\theta}(t,\tilde{x}_{t})^{\ell}\rangle\mathrm{d}t, (178) where x ~ \tilde{x} is the same as x x except that the context is replaced by "Answer" . Given a score S S , we define the accuracy as follows. Given a context s s and possible continuations c ( 1 ) , … , c ( n ) c^{(1)},\dots,c^{(n)} for this context with ground-truth c ( 1 ) c^{(1)} , we define the accuracy as acc = δ 1 ​ ( argmax j ∈ { 1 , … , n } ​ S ​ ( s , c ( j ) ) ) \text{acc}=\updelta_{1}\bigl(\mathrm{argmax}_{j\in\{1,\dots,n\}}S(s,c^{(j)})\bigr) , where we normalize each score by the byte length of its continuation. For each task we report the average accuracy over the test set. The quantity q t q_{t} is the density we consider to reweight the time during training with the ring buffer, see Section J.1 for details. This practice is consistent with the recommendation of Holtzman et al. (2021) who introduced Domain Conditional Pointwise Mutual Information . For completeness, we sweep over w ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] w\in[0,1] and remark that w = 0 w=0 corresponds to disregarding the domain regularization. We first evaluate the results for a checkpoint obtained while training with the hyper-parameters of Section J.6 . However, we note that the training procedure on OWT noises the whole sequence of 1024 tokens. Hence, when we noise only the continuation while keeping the context clean in ( 178 ), the model is severely out of distribution. We therefore also train a short adaptation run, which changes how the sequence is corrupted on OWT. To train the adapted model, we initialize the training run with the baseline weights and train the model for 20,000 iterations with global batch size 256 and EMA decay rate 0.999. We consider a learning rate of 1 × 10 − 4 1\times 10^{-4} with cosine decay to 0 after 20,000 iterations. Finally, during the adaptation run, we train on OWT sequences of length 128 and corrupt them as at evaluation: each sequence is split into a clean context and a noised continuation, with lengths ( L s , L c ) (L_{s},L_{c}) drawn from the 1,024 1{,}024 pairs measured on the tokenized evaluation prompts.

sections.heading: Experimental setup.
sections.text:
We evaluate unconditional de novo molecular generation following the GenMol benchmark protocol ( Lee et al., 2025 ) using the SAFE (Sequential Attachment-based Fragment Embedding) molecular representation ( Noutahi et al., 2024 ) . We train on the SAFE-GPT dataset ( Noutahi et al., 2024 ) (v2 version) using the SAFE tokenizer, which has a vocabulary size of | 𝒱 | = 1,880 |\mathcal{V}|=1{,}880 . All sequences are padded or truncated to a fixed length of L = 256 L=256 . In all diffusion experiments, we treat padding tokens as ordinary tokens during forward corruption, reverse denoising, and in the loss, whereas in the autoregressive (AR) baseline, padding tokens are ignored in the cross-entropy loss. For all experiments, we use a 12 12 -layer BERT ( Devlin et al., 2019 ) transformer ( d model = 768 d_{	ext{model}}=768 , 12 12 attention heads, MLP dimension 3,072 3{,}072 ) similar to the 87 ​ M 87	ext{M} -parameter BERT-Base architecture of GenMol ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . We use Post-LayerNorm layers as in MaskGIT ( Chang et al., 2022 ) , but replace its MLM prediction head with a single zero-initialized linear output layer that is not tied to the input embeddings. For masked diffusion, similar to Sahoo et al. (2024) , we do not condition the network on the diffusion time, while for uniform and Simplex diffusion, we study both variants – with and without time conditioning. Time-conditioned variants use Sinusoidal time embedding with SiLU activation and embedding dimension 128 128 , the time conditioning is provided via adaptive layer normalization (AdaLN). Diffusion models use bidirectional attention, while the AR model uses causal attention. We disable dropout on the attention probabilities and apply a hidden dropout rate of 0.1 0.1 to the embedding output and to every attention and MLP sublayer output. For Simplex Diffusion, the denoiser receives the expectation embedding ( 163 ) of each simplex state. We do not use Self-Conditioning in any of the diffusion models. SDM and masked diffusion are trained with cross-entropy objectives, while uniform diffusion is trained with the ELBO objective. All models are trained for up to 400 400 k iterations with a global batch size of 2,048 2{,}048 using AdamW ( lr = 3 × 10 − 4 	ext{lr}=3	imes 10^{-4} with a 2,500 2{,}500 -step linear warmup followed by a constant schedule, weight decay 0.0 0.0 , β 1 = 0.9 , β 2 = 0.999 , ϵ = 10 − 8  eta_{1}=0.9, eta_{2}=0.999,\epsilon=10^{-8} ), global gradient-norm clipping at 1.0 1.0 , and an EMA of the parameters with decay 0.9999 0.9999 ; all evaluations use the EMA parameters. During training, diffusion times are drawn from [ 10 − 4 , 1 ] [10^{-4},1] : by stratified uniform sampling for MDM and UDM, and by the adaptive time sampler of Section J.1 for SDM. During training, we monitored the evaluation metrics (see below) and noticed that some runs (including AR ones) exhibited collapse (all the evaluation metrics went to zero, while the loss went up). We therefore used early stopping. For each training run, we select the checkpoint with the highest Quality (see below) metric, computed on 1,000 1{,}000 generated molecules. For this evaluation, every method used the standard sampler (see below) with temperature T = 1 T=1 and 256 256 sampling steps, and we used κ = 0 \kappa=0 for Simplex diffusion. The checkpoints were saved every 500 500 steps. In addition, for Simplex Diffusion, we swept over the concentration schedules: Constant-linear ( OPEN ν 0 = 0.2 , ν 1 = 0.5 , ℓ = 0.8 )

sections.heading: Evaluation Metrics.
sections.text: Following Lee et al. (2025) , we generate M = 1,000 M=1{,}000 molecules from scratch for each of 3 3 sampling seeds, and report the mean ± \pm standard deviation over seeds. Generated SAFE strings are decoded using the post-processing from ( Lee et al., 2025 ) . We report four metrics: Validity (percentage of the M M generated sequences that decode to chemically valid molecules), Uniqueness (percentage of unique canonical SMILES among valid molecules), Diversity (one minus the mean pairwise Tanimoto similarity of Morgan fingerprints with radius 2 2 and 2,048 2{,}048 bits, over the unique valid molecules), and Quality (percentage of generated samples that are simultaneously valid, unique and drug-like. Drug-like molecules are defined as those satisfying quantitative estimate of drug-likeness QED ≥ 0.6 \mathrm{QED}\geq 0.6 ( Bickerton et al., 2012 ) and synthetic accessibility SA ≤ 4 \mathrm{SA}\leq 4 ( Ertl & Schuffenhauer, 2009 ) , respectively, following Lee et al. (2025) .).

sections.heading: Sampling and Hyperparameter Sweeps.
sections.text: For the autoregressive (AR) baseline, we generate sequences token-by-token using temperature-scaled softmax sampling with temperature T T . For all diffusion models, we evaluate sampling budgets of { 32 , 64 , 256 , 1024 } \{32,64,256,1024\} steps and three sampling schedules: linear , cosine , and adaptive ( Section J.1 ). The detailed results in Tables 14 and 15 use 256 256 steps. We use two diffusion sampling strategies: (i) standard (ordinary) sampling ( Table 14 ), where all sequence positions at step t → s t\to s are updated solely via the reverse bridge transition kernel using temperature-scaled clean predictions sampled from P ^ 0 ℓ = Softmax ⁡ ( z θ ℓ ​ ( P t ) / T ) \hat{P}_{0}^{\ell}=\operatorname{Softmax}(z_{\theta}^{\ell}(P_{t})/T) (with churn κ ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] \kappa\in[0,1] in Section 3.1 for SDM); (ii) confidence-based ( conf. ) sampling ( Table 15 ), where each position ℓ ∈ { 1 , … , L } \ell\in\{1,\dots,L\} is scored by its maximum predicted probability c ℓ = max v ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ P ^ 0 , v ℓ c_{\ell}=\max_{v\in\mathcal{X}}\hat{P}_{0,v}^{\ell} . At step t → s t\to s , we commit the union of the ⌊ α s p ​ L ⌋ \lfloor\alpha_{s}^{p}L\rfloor most confident positions (top-fraction schedule with power p p ) directly to their most likely token arg ⁡ max v ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ P ^ 0 , v ℓ \arg\max_{v\in\mathcal{X}}\hat{P}_{0,v}^{\ell} (a simplex vertex for SDM). The remaining positions follow the standard update (i). Here, α s \alpha_{s} is defined in ( 2 ) and is evaluated at the target time s s of the transition from t t to s s . Note that the end at the step going from t → s t\to s we have a mixed of clean and noisy tokens in the sample. In the case of UDM and MDM those samples are in distribution while in the case of SDM they are severely out of distribution . Nevertheless we observe benefits from using this confidence based sampler even without retraining. Additional training of the denoiser with such strategy (e.g. training with a fraction α t p \alpha_{t}^{p} of positions replaced by clean vertices) could, in principle, further improve Quality and remains an interesting avenue for future work. For MDM, unmasked tokens are never re-masked, and when the top-fraction schedule is active, positions outside the committed set stay masked. For SDM and UDM, the committed set is recomputed at every step.

sections.heading: K.4 Auto-Guidance on TinyGSM
sections.text: While Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG; Ho & Salimans, 2022 ) is a standard mechanism for improving sample fidelity in diffusion models, it requires training with conditioning dropout and cannot be applied directly to unconditional generation or pre-trained models without dropout tokens. To sharpen generation quality at inference time without modifying the training objective, we adapt Auto-Guidance ( Karras et al., 2024 ) to Simplex Diffusion Models (SDMs). Specifically, we guide the fully converged model θ final \theta_{\text{final}} away from an earlier, unconverged checkpoint θ K \theta_{K} saved during training. More precisely, we modify the logits and probabilities of the Simplex Diffusion Model as follows ζ ~ ​ ( x t , t ) = ζ θ final ​ ( x t , t ) + w ⁡ ( ζ θ final ​ ( x t , t ) − ζ θ K ​ ( x t , t ) ) , p ^ 0 ​ ( x t , t ) = softmax ⁡ ( ζ ~ ​ ( x t , t ) T ) , \tilde{\zeta}(x_{t},t)=\zeta_{\theta_{\text{final}}}(x_{t},t)+w\bigl(\zeta_{\theta_{\text{final}}}(x_{t},t)-\zeta_{\theta_{K}}(x_{t},t)\bigr),\qquad\hat{p}_{0}(x_{t},t)=\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{\tilde{\zeta}(x_{t},t)}{T}\right), (179) where w ≥ 0 w\geq 0 controls the guidance strength ( w = 0 w=0 recovers the un-guided baseline). We apply Auto-Guidance to the TinyGSM SDM with the expected embedding (no SC; ν 0 = 0.2 \nu_{0}=0.2 , ν 1 = 0.5 \nu_{1}=0.5 , ℓ = 0.2 \ell=0.2 ), sampled with 64 steps. The guided model is the EMA checkpoint at 250 250 k steps, and the guiding model uses the raw (non-EMA) parameters at step K ∈ { 0 , 10 ​ k , 20 ​ k , 30 ​ k , 50 ​ k , 100 ​ k , 150 ​ k , 200 ​ k , 249.5 ​ k } K\in\{0,10\text{k},20\text{k},30\text{k},50\text{k},100\text{k},150\text{k},200\text{k},249.5\text{k}\} . We sweep w ∈ { 0.05 , 0.1 , 0.15 , 0.2 , 0.25 , 0.35 , 0.5 , 0.75 , 1.0 , 1.5 } w\in\{0.05,0.1,0.15,0.2,0.25,0.35,0.5,0.75,1.0,1.5\} and logit temperatures T ∈ { 0.01 , 0.1 , 1.0 } T\in\{0.01,0.1,1.0\} for each churn κ ∈ { 0.0 , 0.2 , 1.0 } \kappa\in\{0.0,0.2,1.0\} , with 3 evaluation seeds. Figure 14 shows TinyGSM pass@1 accuracy for w ∈ { 0.1 , 0.25 , 0.5 , 1.0 } w\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5,1.0\} . We observe that guiding against an early-to-intermediate checkpoint ( K ∈ [ 20 ​ k , 50 ​ k ] K\in[20\text{k},50\text{k}] ) maximizes the accuracy for all churn levels κ \kappa , while for checkpoints close to convergence, the accuracy gets closer to the unguided baseline.
